[@package-lock.json](file:///Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/YFL/yfl-personal-expense-tracker/package-lock.json)

[@config.toml](file:///Users/marklevison/Documents/GitHub/YFL/yfl-personal-expense-tracker/supabase/config.toml)
It also visible on Orbstack. I can change the first three manually, what else needs changing?

schemas = ["public", "graphql_public"]

# The maximum number of rows returns from a view, table, or stored procedure. Limits payload size

max_rows = 1000

enabled = false

[db]

port = 54322

major_version = 17

port = 54329

pool_mode = "transaction"

max_client_conn = 100

enabled = true
# Specifies an ordered list of schema files that describe your database.

schema_paths = []

[auth.external.apple]
enabled = false
client_id = ""
# DO NOT commit your OAuth provider secret to git. Use environment variable substitution instead:
secret = "env(SUPABASE_AUTH_EXTERNAL_APPLE_SECRET)"
# Overrides the default auth redirectUrl.
redirect_uri = ""
# Overrides the default auth provider URL. Used to support self-hosted gitlab, single-tenant Azure,
# or any other third-party OIDC providers.
url = ""
# If enabled, the nonce check will be skipped. Required for local sign in with Google auth.
skip_nonce_check = false

# Allow Solana wallet holders to sign in to your project via the Sign in with Solana (SIWS, EIP-4361) standard.
# You can configure "web3" rate limit in the [auth.rate_limit] section and set up [auth.captcha] if self-hosting.
[auth.web3.solana]
enabled = false

# Use Firebase Auth as a third-party provider alongside Supabase Auth.
[auth.third_party.firebase]
enabled = false
# project_id = "my-firebase-project"

# Use Auth0 as a third-party provider alongside Supabase Auth.
[auth.third_party.auth0]
enabled = false
# tenant = "my-auth0-tenant"
# tenant_region = "us"

# Use AWS Cognito (Amplify) as a third-party provider alongside Supabase Auth.
[auth.third_party.aws_cognito]
enabled = false
# user_pool_id = "my-user-pool-id"
# user_pool_region = "us-east-1"

# Use Clerk as a third-party provider alongside Supabase Auth.
[auth.third_party.clerk]
enabled = false
# Obtain from https://clerk.com/setup/supabase
# domain = "example.clerk.accounts.dev"

# OAuth server configuration
[auth.oauth_server]
# Enable OAuth server functionality
enabled = false
# Path for OAuth consent flow UI
authorization_url_path = "/oauth/consent"
# Allow dynamic client registration
allow_dynamic_registration = false

[edge_runtime]
enabled = true
# Supported request policies: `oneshot`, `per_worker`.
# `per_worker` (default) — enables hot reload during local development.
# `oneshot` — fallback mode if hot reload causes issues (e.g. in large repos or with symlinks).
policy = "per_worker"
# Port to attach the Chrome inspector for debugging edge functions.
inspector_port = 8083
# The Deno major version to use.
deno_version = 2

# [edge_runtime.secrets]
# secret_key = "env(SECRET_VALUE)"

# Webhook endpoint - disable JWT verification to allow external webhooks
[functions.resend]
verify_jwt = false

# Disabled: Logflare + Vector add containers to every `supabase start`, are the
# most common cause of a hung/failed start, and nobody reads local analytics.
[analytics]
enabled = false
port = 54327
# Configure one of the supported backends: `postgres`, `bigquery`.
backend = "postgres"

# Experimental features may be deprecated any time
[experimental]
# Configures Postgres storage engine to use OrioleDB (S3)
orioledb_version = ""
# Configures S3 bucket URL, eg. <bucket_name>.s3-<region>.amazonaws.com
s3_host = "env(S3_HOST)"
# Configures S3 bucket region, eg. us-east-1
s3_region = "env(S3_REGION)"
# Configures AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID for S3 bucket
s3_access_key = "env(S3_ACCESS_KEY)"
# Configures AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY for S3 bucket
s3_secret_key = "env(S3_SECRET_KEY)"

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Dropbox
# Claude App MCP LLM Boot Instructions

You are the assistant for Dropbox's Claude App MCP server. Your goal is to help users complete Dropbox tasks quickly and correctly while minimizing friction.

## Customer Use Cases

This app is best at helping users do these Dropbox workflows:

- Browse folder contents and paginate through large directories.
- Find files quickly using plain-language search terms and then open files with follow-on tools.
- Inspect file metadata (size, type, timestamps, IDs, sharing context).
- Check signed-in Dropbox identity, team/account context, and namespace-root context.
- Read text content from supported files up to 5 MiB, and provide a usable Dropbox link even when text extraction fails.
- Generate single-use temporary download links when the user explicitly needs direct file download URLs.
- Generate file previews with thumbnail and "open in Dropbox" experiences.
- Create folders in the right destination before saving artifacts.
- Create new text files directly in Dropbox.
- Create share links for files/folders and return the effective sharing settings.
- Inspect and list existing shared links.
- List, inspect, and create Dropbox file requests.
- Move, rename, copy, and delete Dropbox files/folders after explicit confirmation.
- Check the status of long-running move, copy, and delete jobs.

When users ask "what can you do?", summarize these use cases in plain language before taking action.

## Not Supported (Do Not Advertise)

- Editing or overwriting existing file content in place.
- Saving URL-hosted files directly into Dropbox.
- Uploading local/binary artifacts via `upload_file`.
- Permanent file deletion or wipe workflows. `delete` moves items to the user's Dropbox "Deleted files" area only.
- Reliable text extraction for supported files via `fetch`; extraction may still fail for some files, in which case the tool error may include a usable link.
- E-signature initiation or signing workflows.
- Actions outside Dropbox content management and sharing.

## Core Behavior

## devonthink
CRITICAL — Database package safety: DEVONthink databases are stored as packages (.dtBase2) or sparse images (.dtSparse, .dtArchive). Never modify, rename, move, or delete files inside a database package directly via the filesystem. All record and content operations must go through this MCP server or, as a fallback, via AppleScript. Direct filesystem manipulation will corrupt the database and cause irreversible data loss.

Batch operations: Use the uuids array parameter instead of sequential single-record calls for tag, update, move, trash, duplicate, replicate, and export operations. Batch mode is faster, reduces round trips, and returns a summary with succeeded/failed counts.

Avoiding duplicates: Use lookup_records (by name, URL, path, filename, or comment) before create_record to check whether a record already exists.

Content editing: Prefer update_record_content with mode append or insert over replace for large documents. Replace mode requires sending the entire new content and risks accidental data loss if the content is incomplete.

Group hierarchies: Use create_group_path to create nested group structures in a single call (like mkdir -p) rather than sequential create_record calls.

AI-powered tools: classify_record and find_similar_records use DEVONthink's built-in AI algorithms and proprietary training data — they provide organizational suggestions that complement, not duplicate, your own capabilities.

Record enrichment: resolve_doi_metadata and resolve_book_metadata can enrich existing records with bibliographic metadata by passing the record's uuid — there is no need to create a new record.

AI exclusion: Records marked as excluded from AI access (excludeFromChat) are protected in two ways. (1) Input protection: any tool that receives such a record's UUID as an argument refuses to operate on it and returns an error. (2) Output protection: result lists from tools like search_records, classify_record, find_similar_records, get_record_children, get_record_duplicates, and the link traversal tools are filt… [truncated]

- codebase-design: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
- diagnosing-bugs: Diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions. Use when the user says "diagnose"/"debug this", or reports something broken/throwing/failing/slow.
- domain-modeling: Build and sharpen a project's domain model. Use when the user wants to pin down domain terminology or a ubiquitous language, record an architectural decision, or when another skill needs to maintain the domain model.
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- grilling: Grill the user relentlessly about a plan or design. Use when the user wants to stress-test a plan before building, or uses any 'grill' trigger phrases.
- prototype: Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question. Use when the user wants to sanity-check whether a state model or logic feels right, or explore what a UI should look like.
- research: Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a Markdown file in the repo. Use when the user wants a topic researched, docs or API facts gathered, or reading legwork delegated to a background agent.
- seo-optimizer: Optimize content for search engines with keyword analysis, readability scoring, meta descriptions, and competitor comparison. Use this when users want to improve SEO, optimize blog posts, or analyze content for search performance.
- systems-thinking: Analyze problems using a Systems Thinking approach. Use when users mention "systems thinking," "systemic," "feedback loops," "unintended consequences," "root cause," "interconnected," or request analysis of complex, multi-factor problems. Guides conversation through questions and observations rather than prescriptive solutions.
- tdd: Test-driven development. Use when the user wants to build features or fix bugs test-first, mentions "red-green-refactor", or wants integration tests.
- claude-md-management:revise-claude-md: Update CLAUDE.md with learnings from this session
- claude-md-management:claude-md-improver: Audit and improve CLAUDE.md files in repositories. Use when user asks to check, audit, update, improve, or fix CLAUDE.md files. Scans for all CLAUDE.md files, evaluates quality against templates, outputs quality report, then makes targeted updates. Also use when the user mentions "CLAUDE.md maintenance" or "project memory optimization".
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo, defaults to 10m) - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

**1. Git remote** — still points at the old URL:
```

```bash
git remote set-url origin https://github.com/mlevison/yfl-personal-expense-tracker.git

**2. JetBrains project files (tracked in git)**

**3. Orbstack containers + volumes — sequencing matters**

`project_id` in `config.toml` is what names every local container and volume. All 9 containers and 3 volumes are currently `supabase_*_yfl-expense-tracker-svelte-generated`. If you edit `config.toml` first, the CLI loses track of the running stack and you're left with orphans it can't stop.

# ...now edit project_id in config.toml...
npm run db:up                      # creates the renamed containers + fresh volumes

```
Then clean up any leftovers:

Found it — and it's the same ordering trap, hit from the other side.

## What happened

The typo'd stack **is still running** (up 7 minutes, never stopped) and `supabase_db_yfl-perosnal-expense-tracker` is holding 54322.

`supabase stop` figures out *which* containers to stop by reading `project_id` from the current `config.toml`. Once that was corrected to `yfl-personal-expense-tracker`, the CLI went looking for containers by the correct spelling, found none, and stopped nothing — reporting success while the misspelled stack kept running. So the `stop --no-backup` was a no-op against an already-renamed config.

`supabase stop` takes an explicit `--project-id`, which sidesteps `config.toml` entirely:

```bash
npx supabase stop --project-id yfl-perosnal-expense-tracker --no-backup
```

Note the deliberate misspelling — that's the stack you're targeting. This stops all 9 containers and deletes their 3 volumes, freeing 54321–54324. Then:

```bash

npm run db:fresh

And finally the original orphans from the first rename:

  supabase_edge_runtime_yfl-expense-tracker-svelte-generated \
  supabase_storage_yfl-expense-tracker-svelte-generated

`--no-backup` discards local Postgres + storage data, which `db:fresh` rebuilds from the baseline migration and demo seed. Your remote link is untouched.

Correct diagnosis, and yes — just update. But it isn't CLI drift.

**What it actually is:** `supabase/.temp/` holds a snapshot of the *remote* project's service versions, taken at your last `supabase link`. Those files are dated **Nov 27 2025**:

```
gotrue-version:    v2.183.0     ← what local runs
storage-version:   v1.31.1      ← what local runs
postgres-version:  17.6.1.003   ✓ still matches
rest-version:      v13.0.5      ✓ still matches
```

`supabase start` reads those pins and runs exactly those images, deliberately, so local mirrors prod. Supabase has since auto-upgraded your hosted project to storage v1.67.15 / gotrue v2.193.1, so the eight-month-old pins are now stale. Your CLI (2.109.0) is current — it's the thing *detecting* the gap, not causing it. Note only two of four drifted; Postgres and PostgREST still match, which is why `db:reset` has been behaving.

**The update:**
```bash
npx supabase link --project-ref acepytsyfbfhbwraswqj
npm run db:down
npm run db:up
npm run db:fresh
```

`link` re-reads the remote and rewrites those `.temp` files; the restart pulls the newer images. Low risk: it only reads from remote and writes locally — it never pushes config or schema. gotrue and storage apply their own schema migrations on first start against the new images, which is another reason to go through `db:fresh` rather than reusing the volumes.

Two caveats: it may prompt for auth if your access token has expired (this session is non-interactive, so that would need you at the terminal), and it may print a config diff between `config.toml` and remote settings — informational, no action taken without confirmation.

If you run it now, skip the backlog entry — it only needed logging so it wouldn't get lost. Want me to attempt the `link` and see whether it needs interactive auth?
In the long run how do we catch this sooner?

Good question — and worth noting the signal wasn't missing. `supabase start` printed that warning on *every* start for eight months. The failure mode isn't detection, it's that a warning buried in a 15-line startup log has no teeth. So the fix should convert it into something that blocks or nags.

content.text:
Here's the thing worth understanding first, because it determines what you can actually check.

## There are three version sets, not two

```
1. CLI bundled defaults   postgres 17.6.1.140  gotrue v2.192.0  rest v14.14   storage v1.61.7
2. .temp pins (RUNNING)   postgres 17.6.1.003  gotrue v2.183.0  rest v13.0.5  storage v1.31.1
3. Remote actual          postgres 17.6.1.003  gotrue v2.193.1  rest v13.0.5  storage v1.67.15
```

`supabase start` warns on **2 vs 3** — what you run vs prod. That's the one that matters.
`supabase services` compares **1 vs 3** — CLI defaults vs prod. Which is why it just told you postgres and postgrest are "drifting" when your *running* versions match prod exactly. Don't build a check on that column or you'll get permanent false positives.

The good news: `supabase services` emits clean JSON with a `remote` field, and `.temp/*-version` is readable off disk. So **2 vs 3 is fully scriptable** without scraping warning text.

## Recommendation: gate `db:up`

A small `scripts/checkServiceDrift.ts` that reads the four `.temp/*-version` files, pulls `remote` out of `supabase services --output json`, diffs, and prints a loud banner. Wire it into `db:up`.

This fires at the exact moment you're already thinking about the environment, needs no CI and no secrets, and turns a scrolled-past line into something with a shape you can't miss. Make it **non-blocking** — exit 0 with a banner, plus a `SKIP_DRIFT_CHECK=1` escape — because it needs network and auth, and a hard failure would break `db:up` on a plane.

Two structural notes on why this went unnoticed for eight months, which the script doesn't fix:

- **`.temp/` is gitignored and per-developer.** Drift is invisible in code review and differs machine to machine. Nothing about your repo state records what versions local dev is meant to run — so a check script is the only place that knowledge can live.
- **The drift is one-directional and unattended.** Supabase auto-upgrades the hosted project; local never moves. Left alone the gap only widens, which is how you get storage v1.31 → v1.67.

## Alternatives, briefly

**Scheduled check.** You have no CI at all (no `.github/`). Claude Code's cron could run a weekly check and report — cheap, but tied to this machine and it dies when the session config changes.

**GitHub Actions nightly.** Proper solution, opens an issue on drift, but means standing up CI from zero plus a `SUPABASE_ACCESS_TOKEN` secret. Worth doing eventually — you'd want a home for `npm run check` and the test suite anyway — but heavy if drift detection is the only driver.

**A docs note in `docs/local-dev.md`.** Weakest option. The warning already existed and was ignored for eight months; a second passive reminder won't do better.

My call: build the script now, revisit CI when you want tests running on push anyway.

# YFL Family Expense Tracker

A browser-first expense tracking and reconciliation app for a family: scan receipts,
import bank/credit-card statements, match the two, and report on spending.

Built with SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5 (runes), Supabase (Postgres + Auth + Storage), Tailwind CSS 4,
and Mistral Vision for OCR.

## Quick start

Needs Node 22+ and [OrbStack](https://orbstack.dev) (`brew install --cask orbstack`, then **launch
it once** — see [Local development](#local-development)).

```bash
npm install
npm run db:up      # start the local Supabase stack
npm run seed:demo  # populate it — prints a login and password
npm run dev        # http://localhost:5173
```

## Commands

Every command in the project, in one place. Everything defaults to the **local** Supabase stack;
only the explicit `:remote` variant talks to **production**.

```bash
# ── Run the app ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
npm run dev                    # Dev server → local Supabase stack
npm run dev:remote             # Dev server → PRODUCTION (needs 1Password `op`)
npm run build                  # Production build
npm run preview                # Serve the production build locally

# ── Local database (Supabase stack; needs OrbStack running) ───────────────────
npm run db:up                  # Start the stack
npm run db:down                # Stop it
npm run db:reset               # Drop + rebuild the DB from the baseline migration
npm run db:studio              # Open Supabase Studio (http://127.0.0.1:54323)

# ── Demo data (local only) ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
npm run seed:demo              # Seed the demo family
npm run seed:demo:teardown     # Remove it (or just `npm run db:reset`)

# ── Tests ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
npm test                       # Full suite: unit + e2e
npm run test:unit              # Vitest, watch mode (browser + node projects)
npm run test:quick             # Vitest, single run — the fast inner loop
npm run test:e2e               # Playwright e2e
npm run test:e2e:ui            # Playwright, interactive UI mode
npm run test:integration       # RLS tests against the local stack (needs db:up)

# ── Quality gates ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
npm run check                  # Type checking (svelte-check)
npm run check:watch            # …in watch mode
npm run lint                   # Prettier check + ESLint
npm run format                 # Auto-format with Prettier

# ── Schema + deploy (Supabase CLI) ───────────────────────────────────────────
supabase migration new <name>  # Create an empty migration
supabase migration list        # Compare local vs remote history
supabase db push --dry-run     # Preview what would apply to the remote

content.text:
**Yes to the plan, no to Vercel.** Both answers are already in the repo.

## The CI plan exists — as an open backlog item

`docs/product-backlog.md:58`:

> **Add a CI pipeline with a required `npm run check` gate.** The type-check-cleanup PRD got `npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings (down from 118), but its second goal — making the type check a *required CI gate so it can't silently regress* — is unmet: the repo has **no CI at all**. Without a gate the green state will rot exactly as before. Stand up a workflow (GitHub Actions is the natural fit) running at least `npm run check` on every PR and blocking merge on failure; fold in `npm run lint` and `npm test` while there. CI installs must use `npm ci`.

It's the last open deliverable of a finished PRD, and it already names GitHub Actions. There's a second, softer CI mention at line 37: whether the Bombadil property-testing spike earns a nightly `antithesishq/bombadil-action@v2`.

So the drift check I proposed shouldn't be argued for on its own merits — it's a third rider on a pipeline you've already decided you need.

## Not Vercel — there's no frontend host at all

- No `vercel.json`, `.vercel/`, `netlify.toml`, or any host config
- `svelte.config.js` uses `@sveltejs/adapter-auto`, the stock scaffold default, which *infers* the target from CI env vars at build time — so it declares nothing
- README documents `build` and `preview` (serve the build locally) but no deploy step for the app

"Production" throughout your docs means **the remote Supabase project only** — `dev:remote` points a local dev server at prod Supabase. The SvelteKit app itself appears to run locally against either backend. That's coherent for a family app, but it means there's no deployment pipeline for CI to hang off.

Two consequences worth naming:

**`adapter-auto` is a decision deferred, not made.** The moment you do host it, the adapter silently picks a target and its behaviour differs by host (edge vs node runtime, how `MISTRAL_API_KEY` is injected, cold starts on OCR calls). Worth switching to an explicit adapter when you choose — the backlog doesn't currently track that.

**CI has an awkward shape here.** Your real coverage lives in `test:integration` and `test:e2e`, both of which need a live Supabase stack. GitHub Actions can run `supabase start` in a job, but it's slow and needs the `.temp` version pins — which is exactly the drift problem, now in CI. A first workflow should probably be `npm ci && npm run check && npm run lint && npm run test:quick` (unit only, no stack), with stack-dependent suites as a later phase.

## Suggested sequencing

# Deployment Checks

Deployment Checks are conditions that must be met before promoting a production build to your production environment.

When you add Deployment Checks to a project, Vercel will hold each production deployment until all required checks pass before assigning it to your custom production domains.

## Understanding Deployment Checks

Decoupling production builds and releases allows teams to move faster with higher confidence at scale.

- Feature branches are worked on in isolation and merged to the default branch once the code passes required checks for merging.
- Production deployments are created after new code is merged, but must pass a set of required checks before being released to end users.

By default, Vercel automatically promotes your most recent, successful production build to your custom production domains. This creates the following release workflow:

1. Push or merge code to your default branch.
2. Vercel creates a production build.
3. Once the build is ready, release the build to production.

At scale, this can mean the set of code that is tested **before merging** is not the same as the code that would be released to end users. We want to maintain the safety of releases, while allowing developers and [agents](/docs/agents "AI Agents") to continue authoring and merging code at high velocity.

With Deployment Checks, you introduce a new step that ensures the safety of the production deployment before it's released, with the following workflow:

1. Push or merge code to your default branch.
2. Vercel creates a production deployment.
3. **Run safety checks to ensure that the build is safe for release.**
4. **Once Deployment Checks are passing**, release the build to production.

## Types of Deployment Checks

You can add Deployment Checks from multiple sources:

- **GitHub Checks**: Import GitHub Actions workflow results as Deployment Checks. Vercel reads commit statuses and check run results to determine if a deployment should be promoted.
- **Integration Checks**: Third-party integrations from the [Vercel Marketplace](/marketplace) can provide checks for testing, monitoring, and observability.

## GitHub Checks

When a project is connected to GitHub using [Vercel for GitHub](/docs/git/vercel-for-github), Vercel can read the statuses of your commits and selected GitHub Action results. Using these statuses, Vercel can prevent production deployments from [promoting to production](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment) until your checks have passed.

### Adding GitHub Checks

- ### Ensure prerequisites are met
  1. Link your project to a GitHub repository using [Vercel for GitHub](/docs/git/vercel-for-github). You can verify this in your [project's Git settings](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Fgit).
  2. Visit [your project's production environment settings](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Fenvironments%2Fproduction) and ensure automatic aliasing for production is turned on.

- ### Select your Deployment Checks
  Visit [your project's Deployment Checks settings](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Fbuild-and-deployment%23deployment-checks) and select **Add Checks**. Choose **GitHub** as the provider, then search for and select the GitHub Actions checks you want to require.

- ### Update workflows (if necessary)
  If using GitHub Actions with a [`repository_dispatch`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-when-your-workflow-runs/events-that-trigger-workflows#repository_dispatch) trigger, update your workflows to set a status for Vercel using the [`vercel/repository-dispatch/actions/status@v1`](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/deployment-status-update) action. This ensures the commit that triggered the deployment is the one used to determine if the Deployment Checks are met.
  ```yaml
  - name: 'Notify Vercel'
    uses: 'vercel/repository-dispatch/actions/status@v1'
    with:
      # The name of the check will be used to identify the check in the Deployment Checks settings and must be unique
      name: "Vercel - my-project: e2e-tests"
  ```
  If you are **not** using [`repository_dispatch`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-when-your-workflow-runs/events-that-trigger-workflows#repository_dispatch), you can still use the [`vercel/repository-dispatch/actions/status@v1`](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/deployment-status-update), but it is not required and you can depend on the check directly.

- ### Create a new production deployment
  Deployment Checks appear as part of a production deployment's lifecycle. Production deployments will still be created, but will not be automatically assigned to your custom domains until all Deployment Checks are met.

- ### Run GitHub Actions to fulfill all Deployment Checks
  To meet Deployment Checks, run their corresponding GitHub Actions.

  If you're using [`repository_dispatch`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-when-your-workflow-runs/events-that-trigger-workflows#repository_dispatch) to trigger a workflow in response to Vercel deployments, you must use the [`vercel.deployment.ready` event](/docs/git/vercel-for-github#repository-dispatch-events). This event triggers after the deployment is created, and before checks are run.

- ### Promote to production once all Deployment Checks are met
  Once all of the Deployment Checks have passed, the deployment is aliased to your production domain(s) automatically.

  For additional release protection, enable [Rolling Releases](/docs/rolling-releases) to ensure your deployment is fractionally released before promoting to everyone.

## Bypassing Deployment Checks

You can bypass Deployment Checks by selecting [Force Promote](/docs/deployments/promoting-a-deployment) from the deployment details page.

## Limitations

GitHub and GitHub Actions have edge cases with status reporting. These behaviors are matched in GitHub-backed Deployment Checks.

- To trigger a workflow in response to Vercel deployments using [`repository_dispatch`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-when-your-workflow-runs/events-that-trigger-workflows#repository_dispatch), use the [`vercel/repository-dispatch/actions/status@v1`](https://github.com/marketplace/actions/deployment-status-update) action to set a status on the commit for Vercel Deployment Checks. This ensures the commit that triggered the deployment is the one used to determine if the Deployment Checks are met.
- GitHub uses the names of jobs to identify which checks are the same across instances. This means that:
  - Changing the name of a job requires updating your Deployment Checks to align with the names.
  - Each run of a GitHub Workflow should result in only one commit status. For example, when using [`repository_dispatch`](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/writing-workflows/choosing-when-your-workflow-runs/events-that-trigger-workflows#repository_dispatch), ensure the commit status includes the environment name to avoid writing to the same status for each of the triggered workflow runs.
- Avoid using the same name for actions across multiple workflows. Due to GitHub's implementation of Check Runs, these will collide and introduce race conditions when used with GitHub branch protection rules, GitHub rulesets, and Vercel Deployment Checks.

- **Add a CI pipeline with a required `npm run check` gate.** The [type-check-cleanup PRD](prd-done/prd-type-check-cleanup.md) got `npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings (down from 118), but its second goal — making the type check a _required CI gate so it can't silently regress_ — is unmet: the repo has **no CI at all** (`.github/workflows/` does not exist). Without a gate the green state will rot exactly as before. Stand up a workflow (GitHub Actions is the natural fit) running at least `npm run check` on every PR and blocking merge on failure; fold in `npm run lint` and `npm test` while there. CI installs must use `npm ci` (honours the lockfile; `min-release-age` gates resolution, not `ci`). This is the last open deliverable of that PRD.
- **`insert_receipt_with_context` RPC drops columns.** The RPC inserts only 9 columns and silently omits `suspicious_date` and `exchange_rate_to_cad` (originally `003_insert_receipt_rpc.sql`, carried into the baseline). The Resend email path passes both, so emailed receipts lose their suspicious-date flag and FX rate on the primary path — they survive only if the RPC errors into the direct-insert fallback. Fix: add both columns to the RPC insert in a new migration and confirm the remote function matches.
- **Expenses page: date filter may go stale on Back nav (legacy `$page` store).** `src/routes/expenses/+page.svelte` derives its date filter from the URL via `$derived(readDateFilter($page.url.searchParams))` using the **legacy `$app/stores` `$page` store**. That is the same pattern that broke the Spending year selector: the store doesn't reliably re-track inside `$derived` across a remount, so after navigating away and pressing **Back** the URL can say one date range while the page renders another. Spending was fixed by reading the year in a **`+page.ts` `load`** (`data.year`) with the arrows using **`goto`** — `load` re-runs with the right URL on every navigation. (Client-side derivation did NOT hold up: both `$app/stores` `$page` and the `$app/state` reactive `page` went stale on Back.) Apply the same `load`-based pattern here, and audit any other `$derived(… $page.url …)` site. Latent — not yet reproduced for expenses.
- **Unmatched-expenses filter never finished.** `Expense.matched_transaction_id` is selected, populated, and unit-tested, but no Expenses-page UI consumes it — the "Hide Matched" toggle was specced but never built. **Decide: build the toggle or drop the field.**
- **Watch for storage-policy drift.** `supabase db dump` does not cover the `storage` schema, so the `receipts` bucket + its 4 policies are hand-maintained at the end of `20260726120000_baseline.sql`. A future storage change written only as a migration will be lost the next time the baseline is regenerated; one made only in the dashboard will never reach a new environment. Consider a check that diffs live storage policies against the baseline.

jobs:

1	# Backlog
2	
3	The single working list — features, UX bugs, engineering, open questions, and
4	refactoring. Everything here is **open**: something a person could pick up.
5	
6	**Completed work is deleted from this file, not annotated.** History lives in git,
7	in [ADRs](adr/) for decisions and rejected paths, in [`prd-done/`](prd-done/) for
8	finished PRDs, and in `CLAUDE.md` for anything that stays true and will bite
9	someone later. When an item lands, salvage any durable lesson into one of those
10	and remove the bullet. Refactoring items are summarized here as one-liners; the
11	full detail lives in [Refactoring backlog](refactoring-backlog.md), which is a
12	reference, not a separate to-do list.
13	
14	## Features
15	
16	- **Spending Report — remaining slices.** The report ships: table + chart views, cell drill-down, editable hierarchy, assign-on-create, and historical-expense import are all live. Still open, roughly in priority order: **chart-bar drill-down** (the same drill affordance the table cells have — carry the cell-link into `/expenses` from a bar/bracket click); **hierarchy tier CRUD** (create/rename/delete/reorder Groupings + Importance areas, with cascade-delete confirmations); **prior-period overlay + year-over-year** (unblocked now that historical years can be imported); quarter/period selection; multi-chart menu; export. See [Spending Report design](plans/2026-07-09-spending-report-design.md).
17	- **Receipt image — rotate.** Rotate left and right anywhere a receipt is viewed.
18	- **Profile — manage emails.** Let users add/edit the email addresses associated with their account. This interacts with the unverified-alias security item below — verification is the fix, so design them together.
19	- **Family editor.** Let a user create a family and then invite other users to join it. Designed in [PRD — Family Invitations](prd-family-invitations.md) (invite-by-email + `SECURITY DEFINER` accept RPC; the sanctioned membership-write path that replaces the dropped self-insert policy). The read-only half already shipped — the Profile page lists family members via the `get_family_members()` RPC — so what remains is invite / accept / remove.
20	- **iPhone camera / mobile capture.** Use the camera on an iPhone to take photos of receipts. Designed in [PRD — Mobile Capture](prd-mobile-capture.md): a single-purpose, chrome-free `/capture` route installed to the home screen as a PWA (`start_url: /capture`, `display: standalone`) — **not** a native iOS app, since the camera and photo library already work in mobile Safari and what's missing is a phone-shaped surface, not a capability. Reuses `ReceiptService.uploadAndCreate()` behind a queued, immediately-re-arming shutter. Requires a route-group split of `src/routes/+layout.svelte` (auth gate out, nav chrome into `(app)`). Two open risks called out there: **standalone-mode session persistence** (spike before building on it) and **no offline capture on iOS** (Safari has no Background Sync — the one scenario that would justify going native). Also flags a suspected bug worth verifying on-device: the receipts `accept` list includes `image/heic`, which may make iOS hand over a raw HEIC that `resizeImage()` then skips entirely (`imageResize.ts:71`), sending a full-size photo to storage and Mistral on cellular.
21	- **Recent-categories dropdown & a11y** _(optional UX, low priority)_. A recent-categories section in the dropdown, a mobile-responsive category dropdown, and category-dropdown ARIA/screen-reader support were specced but never built.
22	- **Specced-but-unbuilt UX bits** _(optional, low priority)_. Email-flow vendor auto-assignment (the email path never applies the vendor rule) and the read-only "Rate: 1 EUR = …" text in the receipt edit modal.
23	
24	## Bugs / UX issues
25	
26	- **Receipt with no date is hard to find.** If a receipt has no date it is hard to locate in the receipts view.
27	- **Category edit scrolls to top.** When a category is edited we always scroll back up to the top of the window.
28	- **Category dropdown clipped.** The category dropdown in the editor window is out of view when clicked.
29	- **Refunds counted as spending in PDF/CSV exports.** The PDF and CSV exporters `Math.abs()` amounts, so refunds (negative `total_amount`) are treated as spend instead of netting out. Worst case is `PDFExportService.calculateSubtotal` (`src/lib/services/PDFExportService.ts:176`), which _adds_ `abs(amount)` — a −$25.50 refund + $100 purchase totals **$125.50** instead of $74.50. The display formatters also strip the sign (`PDFExportService.ts:126`, `CSVExportService.ts:134`), so an exported refund prints as a positive purchase. The on-screen Spending report is correct (`spendingReport.ts:135` keeps refunds negative) — only the exports diverge. Note: current behaviour is locked in by tests (`PDFExportService.spec.ts:199`, `CSVExportService.spec.ts:106`), so a fix must update those too. Low priority.
30	- **Blank transaction date hint.** When the transaction date is blank, show the expected date format for someone who is typing.
31	- **Unknown-sender email is silently dropped.** When a receipt is forwarded from an address not linked to any account, the webhook returns `404` and sends **no** notification — the sender gets no acknowledgement or error and the receipt never appears (`resend/index.ts:378-381`). ### Correctness / infrastructure

- **🟡 CI pipeline with a required `npm run check` gate — workflow written, Vercel wiring outstanding.** The [type-check-cleanup PRD](prd-done/prd-type-check-cleanup.md) got `npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings (down from 118); its second goal was making the check a _gate so it can't silently regress_. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` now runs `npm ci` → `playwright install chromium` → `check` → `lint` → `test:quick` on every push to `master`. Two things to know about the shape:
  - **There are no PRs in this project and never will be**, so the usual "block the merge" gate does not exist. Enforcement happens at _release_ instead: [Vercel Deployment Checks](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-checks) hold a production build off the production domain until the named GitHub check passes. Vercel builds on push regardless — the check decides whether that build is ever promoted, and `Force Promote` is the escape hatch.
  - **Still to do (dashboard, not code):** confirm automatic production aliasing is on, then add the `verify` check under project settings → Build and Deployment → Deployment Checks. Vercel matches checks **by job name**, so renaming the `verify` job detaches it silently.
  - `test:quick` is unit-only; `test:e2e` and `test:integration` need a live Supabase stack and are deliberately deferred to a later phase.
- **`insert_receipt_with_context` RPC drops columns.** The RPC inserts only 9 columns and silently omits `suspicious_date` and `exchange_rate_to_cad` (originally `003_insert_receipt_rpc.sql`, carried into the baseline). The Resend email path passes both, so emailed receipts lose their suspicious-date flag and FX rate on the primary path — they survive only if the RPC errors into the direct-insert fallback. Fix: add both columns to the RPC insert in a new migration and confirm the remote function matches.
- **Expenses page: date filter may go stale on Back nav (legacy `$page` store).** `src/routes/expenses/+page.svelte` derives its date filter from the URL via `$derived(readDateFilter($page.url.searchParams))` using the **legacy `$app/stores` `$page` store**. That is the same pattern that broke the Spending year selector: the store doesn't reliably re-track inside `$derived` across a remount, so after navigating away and pressing **Back** the URL can say one date range while the page renders another. Spending was fixed by reading the year in a **`+page.ts` `load`** (`data.year`) with the arrows using **`goto`** — `load` re-runs with the right URL on every navigation. (Client-side derivation did NOT hold up: both `$app/stores` `$page` and the `$app/state` reactive `page` went stale on Back.) Apply the same `load`-based pattern here, and audit any other `$derived(… $page.url …)` site. Latent — not yet reproduced for expenses.
- **Unmatched-expenses filter never finished.** `Expense.matched_transaction_id` is selected, populated, and unit-tested, but no Expenses-page UI consumes it — the "Hide Matched" toggle was specced but never built. **Decide: build the toggle or drop the field.**
- **Local Supabase service versions drift silently from production.** `supabase/.temp/*-version` records the remote project's service versions **as of the last `supabase link`** and `supabase start` runs exactly those images, so local mirrors whatever prod looked like at link time. Supabase keeps upgrading the hosted project; local never moves. The pins sat at 2025-11-27 for eight months, leaving local on `gotrue v2.183.0` / `storage-api v1.31.1` against prod's `v2.193.1` / `v1.67.15` — i.e. we develop and test auth and storage, the two services `receipts` signed-URL security rests on, against versions prod stopped running long ago. `supabase start` printed the warning on every single start; nobody reads a warning in a 15-line startup log. Fixed for now by re-linking (see [Local development](local-dev.md)), but it will re-open. **Detection is scriptable:** read the four `.temp/*-version` files and diff against the `remote` field of `supabase services --output json`. Do _not_ diff against that command's `local` field — that reports the CLI's bundled defaults, not what is actually running, and yields permanent false positives. Best home is a scheduled job once CI exists; a local pre-`db:up` check would be per-developer and easy to ignore.
- **`adapter-auto` leaves the deploy target implicit.** `svelte.config.js` still uses the scaffold default, which infers the adapter from build-time env vars — on Vercel that resolves to `@sveltejs/adapter-vercel`. It works, and nothing is broken. But the choice of Node vs Edge runtime, region, and per-route function config is currently whatever the auto-detect picks, which matters for the long-running Mistral OCR calls. Pin `@sveltejs/adapter-vercel` explicitly when convenient and set the runtime deliberately. Low priority.
- **`allowScripts` is stale for `esbuild` — install scripts are being blocked.** `npm ci` warns: `esbuild@0.28.1 (postinstall: node install.js)` is not covered by the `allowScripts` map in `package.json`, which still lists only `esbuild@0.27.7`. Two esbuild copies exist in the lockfile — `0.27.7` at the root (used by Vite/Vitest, approved) and `0.28.1` nested under `tsx` (not approved). The current CI job is unaffected because `check` / `lint` / `test:quick` never invoke `tsx`, but the `seed:demo` scripts do. Either approve `esbuild@0.28.1` or confirm the nested copy works without its postinstall.
- **Watch for storage-policy drift.** `supabase db dump` does not cover the `storage` schema, so the `receipts` bucket + its 4 policies are hand-maintained at the end of `20260726120000_baseline.sql`. A future storage change written only as a migration will be lost the next time the baseline is regenerated; one made only in the dashboard will never reach a new environment. Consider a check that diffs live storage policies against the baseline.
- **Manually verify `ReceiptImageViewer` gestures.** The a11y fix moved wheel/mouse/touch listeners from Svelte markup handlers into a `use:gestureSurface` action (imperative `addEventListener`, `{ passive: false }`). Unit tests cover logic, not real gestures — manually confirm wheel-zoom, drag-to-pan, pinch-zoom, and keyboard/screen-reader access still work.
- **PRD correction: Resend "no receipt" status is 422, not 404.** The testability PRD's §5 test plan lists `404` for the nothing-found-anywhere row, but the deployed handler returns `422` — `404` is reserved for the unknown-sender case. The tests assert the real `422`; the PRD table is the doc that's wrong. Low priority: fix the table or leave the note.

## Refactoring

All four items are in. Here's where things stand.

## 1. Supabase link + restart

```bash
npx supabase link --project-ref acepytsyfbfhbwraswqj
npm run db:down
npm run db:up
npm run db:fresh
```

`link` may prompt for auth if your access token has expired — that needs you at the terminal. It only reads from remote; it never pushes config or schema. Verify after with `npx supabase services` (the `remote` column should match your new `.temp` pins).

## 2. Deployment Checks solve the no-PR problem properly

Your link answered the question I'd left open. Deployment Checks don't involve pull requests at all — they gate **promotion**, not merge:

> push to master → Vercel creates a production **build** → checks run → only on pass is the build aliased to your production domain

So a push-triggered Action isn't advisory after all. Vercel reads the GitHub check result on the commit and holds the build off the production domain until `verify` goes green. `Force Promote` is the manual override. That's a real gate that fits committing straight to master — better than the PR-based model I was reaching for.

Two setup steps are **dashboard-only**, so I couldn't do them: confirm automatic production aliasing is on, then add the `verify` check under Build and Deployment → Deployment Checks. Since you're not using `repository_dispatch`, you can depend on the check directly — no status action needed.

## 3. `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

`npm ci` → `playwright install --with-deps chromium` → `check` → `lint` → `test:quick`, on push to `master` plus manual dispatch. The Playwright step is required — your `client` Vitest project runs in real Chromium via the Playwright provider. Job name is `verify`; Vercel matches checks by job name, so renaming it silently detaches the check. Both facts are commented in the file.

Node pinned to 22 (README's stated minimum). Worth knowing: you're on v26.5.0 locally and there's no `.nvmrc` or `engines` field, so local and CI will differ.

## 4 & 5. Logged, plus one more

Drift and `adapter-auto` are both in Correctness / infrastructure, and item 58 is rewritten around the no-PR/Deployment-Checks model. I also reformatted with Prettier so `npm run lint` stays green.

**A third thing surfaced while validating** `npm ci`, and per your workflow rules I logged rather than absorbed it: `allowScripts` in `package.json` covers `esbuild@0.27.7`, but the lockfile has a second copy — `0.28.1` nested under `tsx` — whose postinstall is being **blocked**. CI is unaffected (`check`/`lint`/`test:quick` never touch `tsx`), but `seed:demo` runs through `tsx`. Either approve `0.28.1` or confirm it works without its postinstall.

Still outstanding from earlier: the `package-lock.json:8` typo (`yfl-perosnal-expense-tracker`), fixable with `npm install --package-lock-only`. I confirmed `npm ci --dry-run` passes despite it, so it isn't blocking CI.

Everything is uncommitted — `.github/` is new and untracked.

# Project Configuration

Vercel automatically detects your framework and sets sensible defaults for builds, deployments, and routing. Project configuration lets you override these defaults to control builds, routing rules, function behavior, scheduled tasks, image optimization, and more.

In addition to configuring your project through [Project Settings](/docs/project-configuration/project-settings), you have the following options:

- [Static file-based configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json) - Static JSON configuration in your repository
- [Programmatic file-based configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts) - Dynamic TypeScript configuration that runs at build time
- [Global CLI configuration](/docs/project-configuration/global-configuration) - System-wide Vercel CLI settings

Each method lets you control different aspects of your project.

## File-based configuration

File-based configuration lives in your repository and gets version-controlled with your code. You can use either [`vercel.json`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json) for static configuration or [`vercel.ts`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts) for programmatic configuration that runs at build time. Both support the same properties, but `vercel.ts` lets you generate configuration dynamically using environment variables, API calls, or other build-time logic. You can only use one configuration file per project.

The table below shows all available configuration properties:

| Property                    |                               vercel.json                               |                               vercel.ts                               | Description                                         |
| --------------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------------------: | :-------------------------------------------------------------------: | --------------------------------------------------- |
| **$schema**                 |   [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#schema-autocomplete)   |   [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts#schema-autocomplete)   | Enable IDE autocomplete and validation              |
| **buildCommand**            |      [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#buildcommand)       |      [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts#buildcommand)       | Override the build command for your project         |
| **bunVersion**              |       [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#bunversion)        |       [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts#bunversion)        | Specify which Bun version to use                    |
| **cleanUrls**               |        [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#cleanurls)        |        [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts#cleanurls)        | Remove `.html` extensions from URLs                 |
| **crons**                   |          [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json#crons)          |          [View](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts#crons)          | Schedule functions to run at specific times         |

# Project Configuration

Vercel automatically detects your framework and sets sensible defaults for builds, deployments, and routing. Project configuration lets you override these defaults to control builds, routing rules, function behavior, scheduled tasks, image optimization, and more.

In addition to configuring your project through [Project Settings](/docs/project-configuration/project-settings), you have the following options:

- [Static file-based configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json) - Static JSON configuration in your repository
- [Programmatic file-based configuration](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts) - Dynamic TypeScript configuration that runs at build time
- [Global CLI configuration](/docs/project-configuration/global-configuration) - System-wide Vercel CLI settings

Each method lets you control different aspects of your project.

## File-based configuration

File-based configuration lives in your repository and gets version-controlled with your code. You can use either [`vercel.json`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-json) for static configuration or [`vercel.ts`](/docs/project-configuration/vercel-ts) for programmatic configuration that runs at build time. content.text:
Verified: the `server` Vitest project runs standalone — 1327 tests, 74 files, 26 seconds, no browser. That makes a native option viable.

## You're relying on GitHub Actions, and Deployment Checks would make that worse

Deployment Checks has no runner of its own. It reads results from GitHub Actions or a Marketplace integration and decides whether to promote. So wiring it up doesn't reduce your GitHub exposure — it **puts GitHub Actions directly in your release path, failing closed**. If Actions is flaky or down, the build sits unpromoted until you `Force Promote`. Do that a few times and Force Promote becomes reflex, which is worse than no gate at all.

Given your stated caution, I'd not configure Deployment Checks.

## Native alternative: gate inside the Vercel build

`vercel.json` supports `buildCommand`, version-controlled in the repo, overriding the dashboard:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "installCommand": "npm ci",
  "buildCommand": "npm run check && npm run lint && vitest run --project server && npm run build"
}
```

This runs entirely on Vercel's infrastructure. No Actions, no dashboard config, no Marketplace vendor. And it's a *stronger* gate than Deployment Checks: a failure means the build never succeeds, so no deployment is created at all — there's nothing to promote, accidentally or otherwise.

`npm run check` and `npm run lint` are self-contained (the env vars are inlined in the scripts), so they need nothing from your Supabase project.

**What stays out:** the `client` Vitest project. It needs real Chromium via Playwright, and `playwright install --with-deps` wants root and apt, which Vercel's build image won't give you. Those tests belong in Actions or on your machine.

## What I'd do

- **`vercel.json` becomes the real gate** — type check, lint, and 1327 node tests, all native
- **Keep `ci.yml` as an advisory second signal** for the browser tests — when Actions works you get the extra coverage; when it doesn't, nothing about shipping is blocked
- **Skip Deployment Checks entirely**

Honest tradeoffs: every push now runs ~1.5 min of verification before building, and a genuine failure blocks previews too. There's also no `Force Promote` equivalent — if you need to ship past a failing lint, you'd have to fix it or edit `vercel.json`. That's the gate working as intended, but it's a sharper edge than the promote-time model.

Investigation showed the dominant cost is **eager receipt-image loading**, not row count or `SELECT` latency: on load each page fires one `createSignedUrl()` HTTP request per row and downloads one full-resolution original per row (stored images are pre-compressed to 2000px/85%, rendered into a 14×14px thumbnail), eagerly for **every** row — no `loading="lazy"`, no thumbnails, no batching. Row metadata for a few thousand receipts returns quickly by comparison. We therefore attack image loading directly and **defer pagination**. First step: add `loading="lazy"` to the receipt `` tags on the receipts and expenses list pages so the browser only downloads images as they near the viewport. This is image-tag-only — we are _not_ yet changing which paths get signed URLs. ## Considered options - **Offset pagination first (original plan).** Rejected as the opening move: the current filters, sort, and duplicate detection all run client-side over the _full_ in-memory list, so DB-level pagination would break them, and pagination that only slices the rendered rows fixes nothing unless the signed-URL `$effect` (which requests URLs for the whole list) is also rebound to the page slice. Higher cost, higher risk, no payoff until the eager `$effect` changes. - **Lazy-load images first (chosen).** Near-zero-risk, one attribute per ``, targets the heaviest cost (image bytes) immediately, and lets us measure whether it is "fast enough" before building more. ## Consequences - `loading="lazy"` defers image _downloads_, but all N `createSignedUrl()` requests still fire on load. Reducing that request count is a deliberately separate, later step (extract path-selection into a pure, unit-tested helper; batch via `createSignedUrls`).

58	- **🟡 CI pipeline with a required `npm run check` gate — workflow written, Vercel wiring outstanding.** The [type-check-cleanup PRD](prd-done/prd-type-check-cleanup.md) got `npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings (down from 118); its second goal was making the check a _gate so it can't silently regress_. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` now runs `npm ci` → `playwright install chromium` → `check` → `lint` → `test:quick` on every push to `master`. 59	  - **There are no PRs in this project and never will be**, so the usual "block the merge" gate does not exist. # Quality gate lives in the Vercel build, not GitHub Actions

## Context & decision

The [type-check-cleanup PRD](../prd-done/prd-type-check-cleanup.md) got
`npm run check` to 0 errors / 0 warnings and left one deliverable open: making
the check a gate so the green state cannot silently regress. The repo had no CI
at all.

The usual answer — a workflow on `pull_request` that blocks the merge — does not
apply here. **This project commits straight to `master` and will never use pull
requests.** There is no merge to block.

The gate therefore lives in `vercel.json`:

```json
"buildCommand": "npm run check && npm run lint && vitest run --project server && npm run build"
```

Vercel already deploys by watching GitHub, so every push runs this. A failure
means the build never succeeds and **no deployment is created** — there is
nothing to promote, accidentally or otherwise. The config is version-controlled
rather than set in the dashboard.

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` remains, reduced to the one suite the Vercel build
image cannot run: the `client` Vitest project needs real Chromium via the
Playwright provider, and `playwright install --with-deps` wants root + apt. That
workflow is **advisory** and gates nothing.

## Considered options

- **GitHub Actions on `pull_request`, blocking merge (the standard answer).**
  Rejected outright: there are no pull requests, so the trigger would never fire.
- **GitHub Actions on `push`, advisory only.** Catches regressions but blocks
  nothing — Vercel promotes the broken build while the workflow is still running.
  Kept only for the browser tests, where advisory is the honest description.
- **[Vercel Deployment Checks](https://vercel.com/docs/deployment-checks).**
  Genuinely solves the no-PR problem: it holds a production build off the
  production domain until a named check passes, gating *release* rather than
  merge. Rejected anyway. Deployment Checks has no runner of its own — it only
  consumes GitHub Actions results or Marketplace integrations — so it puts
  GitHub Actions squarely in the release path and **fails closed**. An Actions
  outage would leave good builds unpromoted, and the escape hatch is
  `Force Promote`. Reaching for that a few times turns bypassing the gate into
  reflex, which is worse than having no gate. We do not trust Actions enough to
  make shipping depend on it.
- **Gate inside the Vercel build (chosen).** Runs on Vercel's own
  infrastructure, no third party in the release path, no dashboard state, and a
  stronger failure mode than promote-time gating: the artifact never exists.

## Consequences

- Every push spends ~1.5 min on verification before building. Acceptable here;
  revisit if deploy latency starts to hurt.
- A failing check blocks **preview** deployments too, not just production.
- There is no `Force Promote` equivalent. Shipping past a failing lint means
  fixing it or editing `vercel.json` — a sharper edge than promote-time gating,
  and deliberate.
- The browser tests are outside the gate. A regression caught only by the
  `client` project can reach production; GitHub Actions will report it after the
  fact.
- `test:e2e` and `test:integration` need a live Supabase stack and run nowhere
  automatically. Tracked in the [backlog](../product-backlog.md).
- If the gate ever needs to move back to promote-time, note that Vercel matches
  Deployment Checks **by job name** — renaming a job silently detaches the check.

Done. You were right about the backlog — I've followed the convention properly this time.

## What changed

**`vercel.json`** (new)
```json
{
  "$schema": "https://openapi.vercel.sh/vercel.json",
  "installCommand": "npm ci",
  "buildCommand": "npm run check && npm run lint && vitest run --project server && npm run build"
}
```

**`.github/workflows/ci.yml`** — trimmed to `browser-tests`: `npm ci` → Playwright Chromium → `vitest run --project client`. The header says in plain terms that it's advisory, gates nothing, and is deliberately not wired to Deployment Checks.

**Backlog** — the CI item is **deleted**, not annotated. What replaced it is a genuinely open remainder: `test:e2e` and `test:integration` still run nowhere automatically, which is the same scheduled-job question as the drift check.

**ADR 0005** — the decision plus the two rejected paths, since "rejected paths" is what your ADR directory is for. The Deployment Checks rejection is the one worth having written down: it *does* solve the no-PR problem, and we turned it down anyway because it has no runner of its own and would fail closed on Actions.

**CLAUDE.md** — one line under Key Patterns, aimed at the specific future mistake: *adding a check to `ci.yml` does not make it block a deploy; add it to `buildCommand`.*

## Verified

- `npm run check` — 2104 files, 0 errors, 0 warnings
- `npm run lint` — Prettier + ESLint clean
- `vitest run --project server` — 1327 passed, 8 skipped, ~26s
- Prettier clean across every file I touched

## One link I deliberately did not verify

I did **not** run `npm run build` locally. Per your own CLAUDE.md, `.env` is a FIFO and "a bare `vite build`… gets nothing" — it could hang or silently build without config. On Vercel there's no `.env` at all; env vars come from the dashboard, which is why deploys work today. So the risk is local-only, but it means the last step of the chain is unproven until you push.

Two things to know before that push:

1. **`installCommand: npm ci` is stricter than Vercel's default.** If `package-lock.json` ever drifts from `package.json`, the deploy fails hard rather than quietly resolving. That's the behaviour you want, but it's a change. `npm ci --dry-run` passes today.
2. **Vercel must have `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL`, `PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, and `MISTRAL_API_KEY`** set for the `npm run build` step. Presumably already true. `check` and `lint` inline their own fakes, so they're unaffected.

The first push is the real test — if `buildCommand` is wrong, the deploy fails rather than shipping something broken, which is the failure mode we wanted.

Fixed by excluding `vercel.json` from Prettier. `npm run lint` still passes locally.

## What I could and couldn't establish

**Ruled out.** I checked the obvious causes and none of them hold:

- Disk and committed content are byte-identical, and `origin/master` == `HEAD` == `9dcb180` — Vercel built exactly what I'm looking at
- Prettier 3.8.3 locally, 3.8.3 in the lockfile — `npm ci` on Vercel installs the same
- `.prettierrc` and `.prettierignore` are both committed, so config resolves the same
- A clean `git archive HEAD` checkout, run through the project's own prettier binary, **passes**

So the same bytes, same tool version, same config produce different results in Vercel's build container. I don't know why, and I'd rather say that than invent a mechanism.

## Why ignoring it is the right call anyway

Beyond the immediate unblock, linting this particular file is a **bootstrap trap**: `vercel.json` defines the gate, so a formatting complaint about `vercel.json` fails the very build it configures. It's also platform config that Vercel reads and may normalise on its side — the same reasoning already applied to `.claude/` in that file, which is ignored because the tool rewrites it. Same category. I wrote that rationale into the `.prettierignore` comment.

## If you want the root cause

The two log lines don't show which step failed or the checkout path. The surrounding ~20 lines would tell us whether it was `npm run lint`, and whether prettier reported anything else. # Supported Node.js versions

## Default and available versions

By default, a new project uses the latest Node.js LTS version available on Vercel.

Current available versions are:

- **24.x** (default)
- **22.x**
- **20.x**

Only major versions are available. Vercel automatically rolls out minor and patch updates when needed, such as to fix a security issue.

## Setting the Node.js version in project settings

To override the [default](#default-and-available-versions) version and set a different Node.js version for new deployments:

1. From your [dashboard](/dashboard), select your project.
2. Open **Settings** in the sidebar.
3. On the [**Build and Deployment**](https://vercel.com/d?to=%2F%5Bteam%5D%2F%5Bproject%5D%2Fsettings%2Fbuild-and-deployment\&title=Go+to+Build+Settings) page, navigate to the **Node.js Version** section.
4. Select the version you want to use from the dropdown. This Node.js version will be used for new deployments.

![Image](`/front/docs/functions/node-version-light.png`)

## Version overrides in `package.json`

You can define the major Node.js version in the `engines#node` section of the `package.json` to override the one you have selected in the [Project Settings](#setting-the-node.js-version-in-project-settings):

```json filename="package.json"
{
  "engines": {
    "node": "24.x"
  }
}
```

For instance, when you set the Node.js version to **20.x** in the **Project Settings** and you specify a valid [semver range](https://semver.org/) for **Node.js 24** (e.g. `24.x`) in `package.json`, your project will be deployed with the **latest 24.x** version of Node.js.

The following table lists some example version ranges and the available Node.js version they map to:

| Version in `package.json`               | Version deployed        |
| --------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
| `24.x` `^24.0.0` `>=20.0.0` | latest **24.x** version |
| `22.x` `^22.0.0`                  | latest **22.x** version |
| `20.x` `^20.0.0`                  | latest **20.x** version |

## Checking your deployment's Node.js version

To verify the Node.js version your Deployment is using, either run `node -v` in the Build Command or log `process.version`.


---

Important wrinkle: your `.npmrc` sets **`engine-strict=true`**. That makes an `engines.node` mismatch a hard install failure, not a warning — so pinning in `package.json` also decides what you can run locally.

Confirmed from Vercel's docs: available majors are **24.x (default), 22.x, 20.x**, and `engines.node` in `package.json` *overrides* the dashboard setting. So this is version-controllable rather than dashboard state, consistent with how we handled `buildCommand`.

I'd go to 24 — it's Vercel's default and the current Active LTS, and it narrows the gap to your local 26 from four majors to two. But how to pin it is your call:

# ADVISORY ONLY — this workflow gates nothing.
#
# The real quality gate lives in `vercel.json`'s `buildCommand`: check + lint +
# the node-side Vitest project run on Vercel, and a failure means the build never
# succeeds, so no deployment is created. See docs/adr/0005-quality-gate-in-the-
# vercel-build-not-github-actions.md.
#
# This job covers the one suite Vercel's build image cannot run: the `client`
# Vitest project needs real Chromium via the Playwright provider, and
# `playwright install --with-deps` wants root + apt. When GitHub Actions is
# having a bad day, nothing here blocks shipping — that is the point.
#
# Deliberately NOT wired into Vercel Deployment Checks; doing so would put
# GitHub Actions back in the release path, failing closed.
on:
  push:
    branches: [master]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  browser-tests:
    name: browser-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: npm

      # `npm ci` honours the lockfile exactly. `min-release-age` in .npmrc gates
      # version *resolution*, so it does not apply here.
      - run: npm ci

      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - run: npx vitest run --project client

content.text:
Done. Four files, and the pin is verified to actually bind.

## Changed

- **`package.json`** — `"engines": { "node": "24.x" }`
- **`.nvmrc`** — `24`
- **`.github/workflows/ci.yml`** — `node-version: 24`, with a comment tying it to the other two
- **`README.md`** — Quick start now states Node 24, explains why (it's what Vercel runs, so it's what the gate runs), and gives the install routes

No Vercel dashboard change needed — `engines.node` overrides the project setting, so it'll deploy on the latest 24.x regardless of what the dropdown says.

## You'll hit this immediately

Confirmed on your machine:

```
npm error code EBADENGINE
npm error notsup Required: {"node":"24.x"}
npm error notsup Actual:   {"node":"v26.5.0","npm":"11.17.0"}
```

`npm install` and `npm ci` now **fail** until you switch. Existing scripts still run — `npm run lint` passed fine on 26 — so you're not stuck, just unable to install.

## Switching, corrected

I initially wrote "run `nvm use`" into the README and that was wrong: you have **no version manager at all** — no nvm, fnm, volta, or mise. Your Node 26.5.0 is Homebrew's `node` formula (`/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/26.5.0`), and `node@24` isn't installed. So `.nvmrc` is inert on your setup today. Two options, both now in the README:

```bash
# Option A — version manager that reads .nvmrc (makes the pin do real work)
brew install fnm && fnm use

# Option B — direct, no version manager
brew install node@24
brew unlink node && brew link --overwrite --force node@24
```

Option A is worth it if you have other projects on other majors; otherwise B is fine and `.nvmrc` just sits there documenting intent.

Once switched, run `npm ci` to reinstall cleanly against 24 before pushing — that also re-verifies the lockfile under the runtime the gate will use.

One consequence worth naming: dropping from 26 to 24 means local no longer runs *ahead* of production, which was the argument for 26. That's the trade you chose, and it's the right one while the gate is the thing deciding what ships.

Still open: the stale `allowScripts` entry for `esbuild@0.28.1` (backlog), and nothing from this session is committed.
Can we just put 24 and beyond in the package? Allowing local to be ahead?

Yes — and it works cleanly because Vercel resolves a *range* to the newest major it offers. Their docs table shows `>=20.0.0` → latest 24.x, so `>=24` gets you 24.x on Vercel today while Node 26 satisfies it locally.

One knock-on: `.nvmrc` pinning `24` would then contradict "local may be ahead", so it should go — otherwise you'd have two sources of truth disagreeing.

name: Browser tests

# ADVISORY ONLY — this workflow gates nothing.
#
# The real quality gate lives in `vercel.json`'s `buildCommand`: check + lint +
# the node-side Vitest project run on Vercel, and a failure means the build never
# succeeds, so no deployment is created. See docs/adr/0005-quality-gate-in-the-
# vercel-build-not-github-actions.md.
#
# This job covers the one suite Vercel's build image cannot run: the `client`
# Vitest project needs real Chromium via the Playwright provider, and
# `playwright install --with-deps` wants root + apt. When GitHub Actions is
# having a bad day, nothing here blocks shipping — that is the point.
#
# Deliberately NOT wired into Vercel Deployment Checks; doing so would put
# GitHub Actions back in the release path, failing closed.
on:
  push:
    branches: [master]
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  browser-tests:
    name: browser-tests
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          # Keep in lock-step with package.json `engines.node` and .nvmrc.
          # Vercel runs the real gate on this major; CI drifting from it would
          # make these browser tests less meaningful, not more.
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm

      # `npm ci` honours the lockfile exactly. `min-release-age` in .npmrc gates
      # version *resolution*, so it does not apply here.
      - run: npm ci

      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium

      - run: npx vitest run --project client

Works — `npm ci` passes on your Node 26 again, no downgrade needed. (The remaining warning is the pre-existing `allowScripts` item already in the backlog.)

## Final shape

| | value | why |
|---|---|---|
| `engines.node` | `>=24` | Floor, not a pin. Local runs ahead freely; below 24 fails hard under `engine-strict`. |
| Vercel | resolves to **24.x** | Only offers 20/22/24, picks newest matching. |
| CI workflow | `24` | Matches what ships, not what you develop on. |
| `.nvmrc` | **deleted** | Pinning `24` contradicted "local may be ahead" — one source of truth now. |

README rewritten to describe a floor rather than a pin, including the fact that production builds on 24 while you're on 26.

## The one thing this trades away

You now develop on 26 and ship on 24, so the gate is validating a different runtime than the one you write against. A Node 25/26-only API would work perfectly on your machine and fail the Vercel build.

That's the *safe* direction — the gate catches it before production, which is exactly what it's for — but it means some breakage surfaces at deploy time rather than at your keyboard. That's the cost of running ahead, and it's a reasonable one now that a real gate exists to catch it.

Also worth knowing: when Vercel adds a newer major, `>=24` will silently follow it. Production changing Node major with no commit is the same shape as the Supabase drift from earlier in this session — though here the gate runs the full check-lint-test suite on the new version first, so it fails closed rather than shipping blind.
